issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette: Mr. Johnson is a 65-year-old African American man who has been struggling with the aftermath of a devastating natural disaster that occurred several months ago. He works at a local retail store and is married to his lifelong partner, Mary. The traumatic event, which was a catastrophic hurricane that destroyed much of their neighborhood, left Mr. Johnson deeply shaken. The night of the hurricane, strong winds ripped through their home with such force that it felt as if the structure itself would collapse at any moment. Debris flew through the air like projectiles, and the roar of the wind was deafening. Mr. Johnson's memories of that terrifying event play out in his mind like a film, replaying over and over again. When he remembers those moments, they feel so vivid that it is as if the hurricane is happening right now. Mr. Johnson has come to believe that the world is inherently dangerous and that he must always be on guard. This belief has led him to adopt several maladaptive strategies to cope with his heightened sense of threat. He constantly checks his surroundings for any signs of danger, making sure to stay close to exits wherever he goes. At work, this means that he often finds himself near the entrance or exit doors, scanning the environment for anything unusual. This hypervigilance and constant need to stay alert also affects his ability to sleep; he has difficulty falling asleep because he feels compelled to remain vigilant throughout the night. Mary has noticed changes in Mr. Johnson’s behavior over time. He avoids situations where he might feel trapped or unable to escape quickly, which has led him to avoid gatherings with friends and family. His constant scanning for exits and keeping his surroundings under close watch is a direct response to his belief that the world is dangerous and unpredictable. Mr. Johnson's recurring memories of the hurricane have only reinforced his negative appraisals about the permanence of damage he believes he has suffered. He feels like the trauma has permanently changed him for the worse, making it harder for him to engage in activities that once brought him joy. When he relives the event, the memory feels so present and real that it heightens his sense of threat and danger. His hypervigilance is not only a response but also feeds into his negative appraisals. The more he scans his environment for signs of potential threats, the more convinced he becomes that danger lurks everywhere. This cycle has made it difficult for him to function normally in his daily life. At work, Mr. Johnson's preoccupation with staying near exits and constantly checking his surroundings has affected his ability to focus on tasks, leading to increased stress and conflict with his colleagues. Mr. Johnson’s fear of reliving the traumatic event is so intense that he often distracts himself by focusing on other activities or thoughts. However, this only provides temporary relief; the memories eventually resurface, triggering a renewed sense of threat and hypervigilance. The culmination of these experiences has left Mr. Johnson feeling isolated and overwhelmed. His relationships with Mary and his coworkers have been strained due to his avoidance behaviors and constant vigilance. The final straw was when he had an episode at work where he nearly triggered a panic among other employees by overreacting to what seemed like a minor incident. Mr. Johnson finally sought help because he is afraid that these symptoms will continue to worsen, potentially leading to more severe consequences in his personal and professional life. He hopes for relief from the constant vigilance and the haunting memories of the hurricane, and believes therapy might offer him a way out of this cycle of fear and avoidance. In summary, Mr. Johnson’s negative appraisals have led him to adopt maladaptive strategies that reinforce his sense of threat and exacerbate his traumatic memories. The interplay between these components has created a self-perpetuating loop that he hopes can be broken through therapeutic intervention.
